processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea. Its best-known use is Oriental Beauty, heavily oxidised after leafhoppers have fed on the buds, with an extra resting step under cloth after pan-firing.
harvest_season: For Oriental Beauty, early summer, around June to July, once leafhoppers have fed on the shoots.
appearance_dry: As Oriental Beauty, twisted or ball-shaped leaf in mixed white, green, yellow, red and brown, with plump pale tips.
appearance_liquor: As Oriental Beauty, amber to deep reddish amber, darker with heavier roasting.
appearance_wet: As Oriental Beauty, a small soft bud and leaf in mixed green and reddish brown.
taste_profile: As Oriental Beauty, strong honey and ripe fruit with no real bitterness or grassy edge.

brewing.notes: Settings for Oriental Beauty, the main tea made from it. Slightly cooler water protects the delicate buds.

vintage_note: The cultivar itself is rarely on the label. Oriental Beauty made from it is sold by the current year's summer harvest. Ask which cultivar was used, because several are.
description:
Qing Xin Da Pan is a Taiwanese tea cultivar and the workhorse of Oriental Beauty in Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Miaoli. The second half of the name is awkward: the character 冇 is rendered in several ways, so you will see Dapan, Da Mao and other spellings.

It is often confused with Qing Xin Wulong, which is a different plant. Both are used for Oriental Beauty, with Qing Xin Wulong the main choice around Pinglin, Shiding and Lugu, and some consider that version the finest.

As Oriental Beauty it gives honey and ripe fruit in an amber cup. The flavour depends on leafhoppers feeding on the shoots, so farmers in areas such as Longtan keep away from pesticides on this tea. Slightly cooler water and medium steeps work well.

When buying, the cultivar is a question worth asking, since sellers often list only the tea's name. A Hsinchu or Miaoli lot may be from this plant, but it is not guaranteed.
history:
The cultivar's origin and early history are poorly recorded. It is best known through the Hakka tea country of Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Miaoli, where it became the main plant for Oriental Beauty.

It also appears as a reference point in Taiwanese breeding: Jin Xuan, released in 1981, is said to yield 20 to 50 percent more than both this cultivar and Qing Xin Wulong. Si Ji Chun is sometimes described as a natural hybrid involving it, though that is told as likely rather than proven.
